questions.subject: JAVASCRIPT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret JavaScript behavior demonstrated by a short executable snippet involving objects — keys.

answer.exemplar: Object.keys returns the enumerable own property names, which are a, b and c, so its length is three. Values such as 3694 do not affect the count. The result is 3.

questions.explanation: Object.keys returns the enumerable own property names, which are a, b and c, so its length is three. Values such as 3694 do not affect the count. A complete answer names 3 and justifies it from the code rather than guessing.
questions.hint: keys returns names, not the stored values.

questions.subject: JAVASCRIPT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret JavaScript behavior demonstrated by a short executable snippet involving objects — destructuring.
questions.explanation: Destructuring binds a to 3695 and b to 2 by matching property names, so their sum is 3697. Order in the pattern does not matter for objects. Carrying the operation through gives 3697; common slips include using only the first destructured field and using only the second field.
questions.hint: Object destructuring matches by property name.

questions.subject: JAVASCRIPT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret JavaScript behavior demonstrated by a short executable snippet involving arrays — spread.

options.misconception: Assuming the spread discards the extra value
Counting the spread as adding two values

questions.explanation: The spread expands the two existing entries and the trailing value is appended, giving 3 elements. The spread form creates a fresh array rather than mutating arr. The printed value is 3, while the alternatives come from assuming the spread discards the extra value, counting the spread as adding two values and reporting only the appended element.
questions.hint: Spread copies existing items before the new one is added.

questions.subject: JAVASCRIPT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret JavaScript behavior demonstrated by a short executable snippet involving functions — rest.

stimulus.body: A program is processing the value 3697.

questions.explanation: The rest parameter gathers every argument after the named one into an array, holding 2, 3 and 4, so its length is three. The leading value 3697 is bound to first. The printed value is 3, while the alternatives come from counting all arguments including first, counting only the last argument and assuming rest parameters collect nothing.
questions.hint: Rest collects arguments left after the fixed parameters.

questions.subject: JAVASCRIPT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret JavaScript behavior demonstrated by a short executable snippet involving functions — hoisting.
questions.explanation: Function declarations are hoisted with their bodies, so typeof reports 'function' even before the source line. Their value is available throughout the enclosing scope. The printed value is function, while the alternatives come from assuming declarations are not hoisted, expecting the return value instead and thinking the early reference throws.
questions.hint: Declarations, unlike expressions, are initialized during hoisting.

questions.learningObjective: Interpret JavaScript behavior demonstrated by a short executable snippet involving functions — closures.

answer.exemplar: The closure keeps n alive between calls; the first invocation raises it to 3700 and the second to 3701. Each call mutates the same captured binding. The result is 3701.

questions.explanation: The closure keeps n alive between calls; the first invocation raises it to 3700 and the second to 3701. Each call mutates the same captured binding. A complete answer names 3701 and justifies it from the code rather than guessing.
questions.hint: A closure retains the variable, it does not copy it per call.
